t.1.3: Behold, O teacher, this mighty army of the sons of Pāṇḍu, arrayed for battle by the son of Drupada, your wise disciple.
t.1.1: Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: On the field of dharma, on the field of the Kurus, gathered together and eager to fight, what did my sons and the sons of Pāṇḍu do, O Sañjaya?
t.1.4: Here are heroes, mighty archers equal in battle to Bhīma and Arjuna: Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa, and Drupada, the great chariot-warrior.
t.1.2: Saṃjaya said: Then, having seen the army of the Pāṇḍavas drawn up in battle array, King Duryodhana approached his teacher and spoke these words.
t.1.5: Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna, and the valiant king of Kāśi; Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Śaibya, a bull among men.
t.1.6: The valiant Yudhāmanyu and the mighty Uttamaujā, Saubhadra and the sons of Draupadī, all of them are indeed great chariot-warriors.
t.1.7: But know also those who are most distinguished among us, O best of the twice-born, the leaders of my army; I name them to you for your recognition.
t.1.8: Your honored self, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, and Kṛpa, ever victorious in battle; Aśvatthāmā, Vikarṇa, and likewise the son of Somadatta.
t.1.9: And many other heroes, who have given up their lives for my sake, armed with various weapons and missiles, are all skilled in warfare.
t.1.10: That army of ours, protected by Bhīṣma, is unlimited, whereas this army of theirs, protected by Bhīma, is limited.
t.1.11: Stationed in all the lines of approach, each in his allotted place, all of you, sirs, must guard Bhīṣma above all.
t.1.12: Then the mighty grandsire, the eldest of the Kurus, roared loudly like a lion and blew his conch, bringing joy to him.
t.1.13: Then conchs and kettledrums, tabors, drums and cow-horns were all at once struck up, and that sound became tumultuous.
t.1.14: Then Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava, stationed in a great chariot yoked with white horses, blew their divine conches.
t.1.15: Hṛṣīkeśa blew the Pāñcajanya, Dhanaṃjaya the Devadatta, and Vṛkodara, of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Pauṇḍra.
t.1.16: King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, blew the Anantavijaya, and Nakula and Sahadeva blew the Sughoṣa and the Maṇipuṣpaka.
t.1.17: The king of Kāśī, a supreme archer, and Śikhaṇḍī, the great chariot-warrior, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Virāṭa, and the unconquered Sātyaki,
t.1.19: That tumultuous uproar, making the sky and the earth resound, rent the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
t.1.20: Then, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra drawn up in battle array, as the clash of weapons was about to begin, the son of Pāṇḍu, whose banner bore the monkey, raised his bow.
t.1.21: Then, O lord of the earth, he spoke these words to Hṛṣīkeśa: "Place my chariot between the two armies, O Acyuta."
t.1.18: Drupada and the sons of Draupadī, O lord of the earth, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā, all of them on every side, blew their conch shells, each his own.
t.1.22: So that I may behold these who stand arrayed, eager to fight, and know with whom I must contend in this undertaking of battle.
t.1.23: I wish to observe those who are about to fight, those who have assembled here, eager to do in battle what is pleasing to the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
t.1.24: Thus addressed by Guḍākeśa, O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa, having stationed the finest of chariots in the middle between the two armies,
t.1.25: In front of Bhīṣma and Droṇa and of all the rulers of the earth, he said: "Pārtha, behold these Kurus assembled here."
t.1.26: There Pārtha saw, standing in place, fathers and also grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and likewise friends.
t.1.28: Overcome by deep compassion and sinking in despair, he spoke thus: "O Kṛṣṇa, seeing these my own kinsmen standing arrayed here, eager to fight,"
t.1.29: My limbs sink and give way, and my mouth is completely parched; a trembling arises in my body, and my hair stands on end.
t.1.30: Gāṇḍīva slips from my hand, and my skin is burning all over; I am unable to stand steady, and my mind seems to whirl.
t.1.31: And I see adverse omens, O Keśava, nor do I foresee any good in slaying my own kinsmen in battle.
t.1.32: I do not desire victory, O Kṛṣṇa, nor kingdom, nor pleasures. Of what use to us is a kingdom, O Govinda, of what use are enjoyments, or even life itself?
t.1.27: Fathers-in-law and friends as well, in both the armies. Having looked upon all those kinsmen standing arrayed there, the son of Kuntī...
t.1.33: Those for whose sake we desired kingdom, enjoyments and pleasures, these very ones stand here arrayed in battle, having given up their lives and their wealth.
t.1.34: Teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other kinsmen as well.
t.1.35: These I do not wish to kill, O Madhusūdana, even though they are killing me, not even for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds; how much less, then, for the sake of the earth?
t.1.36: Having slain the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, what joy could be ours, O Janārdana? Sin alone would cling to us for killing these aggressors.
t.1.37: Therefore we ought not to kill the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with their kinsmen; for how could we be happy, O Mādhava, after killing our own people?
t.1.38: Even if these men, their minds overpowered by greed, do not see the wrong caused by the destruction of a family, nor the sin in treachery toward friends.
t.1.39: Why should we not know to turn back from this sin, O Janārdana, we who clearly see the wrong caused by the destruction of a family?
t.1.40: With the destruction of the family, the eternal family dharmas perish; and when dharma is lost, adharma overpowers the entire family.
t.1.41: From the predominance of adharma, O Kṛṣṇa, the women of the family become corrupted; and when the women are corrupted, O Vārṣṇeya, there arises a mixing of varṇas.
t.1.43: By these misdeeds of the destroyers of the family, which bring about the confusion of varṇas, the eternal duties of caste and the duties of the family are destroyed.
t.1.42: This intermixture leads only to hell, for the destroyers of the family and for the family itself; for their ancestors fall, deprived of the rites of offering rice-balls and water.
t.1.44: O Janārdana, we have heard it said that for men whose family dharma has been destroyed, a dwelling in hell is certain.
t.1.45: Alas, alas! We have resolved to commit a great sin, in that, through greed for the pleasures of kingship, we are prepared to slay our own kinsmen.
t.1.46: If the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, weapons in hand, were to slay me in battle, unresisting and unarmed, that would be better for me.
t.1.47: Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna cast aside his bow together with its arrows and sat down on the seat of the chariot, his mind overwhelmed with grief.
t.2.1: Saṃjaya said: To him, thus overcome with pity, his eyes troubled and filled with tears, and sinking in despair, Madhusūdana spoke these words.
t.2.2: The Blessed Lord said: Whence has this weakness come upon you in this hour of crisis, O Arjuna? It is not practiced by the noble, it does not lead to heaven, and it brings disgrace.
t.2.3: Do not yield to unmanliness, Pārtha; it does not befit you. Cast off this petty weakness of heart and arise, scorcher of foes!
t.2.4: Arjuna said: O Madhusūdana, how shall I fight back with arrows in battle against Bhīṣma and Droṇa, who are both worthy of worship, O slayer of enemies?
t.2.5: Better indeed to eat even alms-food here in this world than to slay these noble-souled teachers; for having slain my teachers, though they are bent on gain, I would here enjoy only pleasures smeared with blood.
t.2.7: My very nature stricken by the fault of faint-hearted pity, my mind utterly confused about dharma, I ask you: tell me decisively what would be better. I am your disciple; instruct me, who have taken refuge in you.
t.2.6: Nor do we know which is better for us, whether we should conquer them or whether they should conquer us. The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra stand before us, the very ones after slaying whom we would not wish to live.
t.2.8: For I do not see what could drive away this grief of mine that dries up my senses, even if I were to obtain on earth an unrivaled, prosperous kingdom, and even sovereignty over the gods.
t.2.9: Sañjaya said: Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, O scorcher of foes, Guḍākeśa said to Govinda, "I will not fight," and fell silent.
t.2.10: O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa, as if smiling, spoke these words to him who was despondent in the midst of both armies.
t.2.11: The Blessed Lord said: You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for, and yet you speak words of wisdom. The wise grieve neither for those whose life has departed nor for those whose life has not departed.
t.2.12: Never was there a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these lords of men; nor shall any of us ever cease to be hereafter.
t.2.13: Just as, for the embodied one, there are childhood, youth and old age in this body, so too there is the attainment of another body; the steadfast one is not deluded by this.
t.2.14: But the contacts of the senses with their objects, O Kaunteya, give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain; they come and go and are impermanent. Endure them, O Bhārata.
t.2.15: O bull among men, the steadfast person whom these do not disturb, who remains the same in sorrow and in joy, is fit for immortality.
t.2.16: Of the unreal there is no being, and of the real there is no non-being; the final truth of both of these has been seen by the seers of reality.
t.2.17: But know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded. No one can bring about the destruction of this imperishable one.
t.2.18: These bodies of the eternal embodied one, who is imperishable and immeasurable, are said to have an end. Therefore fight, O Bhārata.
t.2.19: He who thinks this one to be a slayer, and he who thinks this one to be slain, both of them do not understand: this one neither slays nor is slain.
t.2.20: He is never born, nor does he ever die; nor, having come to be, will he ever cease to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting and primeval, he is not slain when the body is slain.
t.2.21: He who knows this to be indestructible, eternal, unborn and imperishable, how, O Pārtha, can that person cause anyone to be slain, or slay anyone?
t.2.22: Just as a man casts off worn-out garments and takes on other, new ones, so the embodied one casts off worn-out bodies and enters into others that are new.
t.2.23: Weapons do not cut this one, fire does not burn this one, waters do not wet this one, and wind does not dry it up.
t.2.24: This Self cannot be cut, this cannot be burned, cannot be wetted, and cannot be dried. It is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and everlasting.
t.2.25: This is said to be unmanifest, this is unthinkable, this is unchangeable. Therefore, knowing this to be so, you should not grieve.
t.2.26: And even if you think of this self as constantly born and constantly dying, even then, O mighty-armed one, you ought not to grieve for it.
t.2.27: For death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died. Therefore, over a matter that cannot be avoided, you ought not to grieve.
t.2.28: Beings are unmanifest in their beginning, manifest in their middle, and unmanifest again in their end, O Bhārata; what lamentation can there be over this?
t.2.29: One sees him as a wonder, another likewise speaks of him as a wonder, and another hears of him as a wonder; yet even having heard of him, no one knows him at all.
t.2.30: This embodied one dwelling in the body of everyone is eternally unslayable, O Bhārata; therefore you ought not to grieve for any creatures.
t.2.31: And considering your own duty as well, you ought not to waver, for there exists nothing better for a kṣatriya than a righteous war.
t.2.33: But if you will not fight this righteous battle, then, having abandoned your own duty and your honor, you will incur sin.
t.2.34: Moreover, all beings will speak of your undying disgrace, and for one who has been held in honor, disgrace is worse than death.
t.2.32: Happy are the kṣatriyas, O Pārtha, who obtain such a battle, come of its own accord, an open door to heaven.
t.2.35: The great chariot-warriors will think that you withdrew from battle out of fear, and you, having been highly esteemed by them, will fall into lightness.
t.2.36: Your enemies will speak many words that ought not to be spoken, disparaging your ability. What, indeed, could be more painful than that?
t.2.37: Slain, you will attain heaven; victorious, you will enjoy the earth. Therefore arise, O Kaunteya, resolved upon battle.
t.2.38: Treating alike pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat, then gird yourself for battle; thus you will not incur sin.
t.2.39: This understanding has been declared to you in terms of Sāṃkhya; now hear it in terms of Yoga, O Pārtha, for joined with this understanding you will cast off the bondage of action.
t.2.40: Here no effort that is begun is ever lost, and no adverse result is found. Even a very little of this dharma protects one from great fear.
t.2.41: Here, O Kurunandana, the resolute understanding is one, but many-branched and endless are the understandings of the irresolute.
t.2.42: O Pārtha, the unwise, who delight in the words of the Veda and declare that there is nothing else, utter this flowery speech.
t.2.44: For those who cling to pleasure and power, whose minds are carried away by that flowery speech, the resolute understanding is not established in samādhi.
t.2.43: Their minds full of desire and heaven their highest goal, they proclaim a speech that offers rebirth as the fruit of action, abounds in elaborate rites, and aims at the attainment of pleasure and power.
t.2.45: The Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain; be free of the three guṇas, Arjuna, free from the pairs of opposites, ever established in sattva, free from concern for acquiring and keeping, and possessed of the Self.
t.2.46: As much use as there is in a small well when there is water flooding on every side, so much use is there in all the Vedas for a brāhmaṇa who truly knows.
t.2.47: Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruits of action be your motive, and let there be no attachment in you to inaction.
t.2.48: Established in yoga, perform your actions, Dhanaṃjaya, having abandoned attachment and having become even-minded in success and failure; evenness of mind is called yoga.
t.2.49: Far inferior indeed is action to the yoga of understanding, O Dhanaṃjaya; seek refuge in understanding. Pitiable are those whose motive is the fruit.
t.2.50: One who is yoked to understanding casts off, here in this world, both good deeds and evil deeds. Therefore, yoke yourself to yoga; yoga is skill in actions.
t.2.51: For the wise, yoked to understanding, having abandoned the fruit born of action and freed from the bondage of birth, go to the state beyond all sorrow.
t.2.52: When your intellect crosses beyond the thicket of delusion, then you will attain indifference toward what is yet to be heard and what has already been heard.
t.2.53: When your understanding, now bewildered by what you have heard of scripture, stands firm and unwavering, immovable in samādhi, then you will attain yoga.
t.2.54: Arjuna said: O Keśava, what is the description of one whose wisdom is steady, who is established in samādhi? How does one of steady mind speak, how does he sit, and how does he walk?
t.2.55: The Blessed Lord said: When one wholly casts off all the desires that have entered the mind, O Pārtha, and is content in the Self by the Self alone, then he is called one of steady wisdom.
t.2.56: One whose mind is not shaken amid sorrows, who is free from craving amid pleasures, and from whom passion, fear and anger have departed, is called a sage of steady wisdom.
t.2.57: He who is without attachment everywhere, who, on meeting with this or that, good or evil, neither rejoices nor hates, his wisdom is firmly established.
t.2.58: When he withdraws his senses from the objects of the senses on every side, as a tortoise draws in its limbs, then his wisdom is firmly established.
t.2.59: The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied one who abstains from them, but the taste for them remains; yet even that taste of his turns away once he has seen the Supreme.
t.2.60: For even of a discerning man who strives, O Kaunteya, the turbulent senses forcibly carry away the mind.
t.2.61: Having restrained them all, he should sit disciplined, intent on me; for he whose senses are under control, his wisdom is firmly established.
t.2.62: For a man who dwells on the objects of the senses, attachment to them arises; from attachment desire is born, and from desire anger springs forth.
t.2.63: From anger arises delusion; from delusion, confusion of memory; from the loss of memory, the destruction of intelligence; and with the destruction of intelligence, one perishes.
t.2.64: But the self-controlled one, moving among the objects of sense with senses freed from attachment and aversion and governed by the self, attains serenity.
t.2.65: In serenity, the destruction of all his sorrows comes about; for the understanding of one whose mind is serene quickly becomes firmly established.
t.2.66: For one who is not disciplined there is no understanding, and for the undisciplined there is no contemplation; for one who does not contemplate there is no peace, and for one without peace, whence can happiness come?
t.2.67: For when the mind is made to follow the roving senses, it carries away his wisdom, as the wind carries away a ship on the waters.
t.2.68: Therefore, O mighty-armed one, he whose senses are completely restrained from the objects of the senses, his wisdom is firmly established.
t.2.69: What is night for all beings, in that the self-controlled one is awake; that in which beings are awake is night for the seeing sage.
t.2.70: As the waters enter the ocean, which is ever being filled yet remains unmoved in its foundation, so the one whom all desires enter in the same way attains peace, not the one who longs after desires.
t.2.71: The man who, having abandoned all desires, moves about free from longing, without the sense of 'mine' and without ego, attains peace.
t.2.72: This, O Pārtha, is the state of Brahman; having attained it, one is no longer deluded. Abiding in it even at the time of death, one reaches the nirvāṇa of Brahman.
t.3.1: Arjuna said: If you hold that understanding is superior to action, O Janārdana, then why do you urge me into this terrible deed, O Keśava?
t.3.3: The Blessed Lord said: In this world a twofold path was taught by me of old, O sinless one: for the Sāṃkhyas the yoga of knowledge, and for the yogins the yoga of action.
t.3.2: With words that seem mixed and contradictory, you seem to bewilder my understanding. Tell me decisively that one thing by which I may attain the highest good.
t.3.4: Not by abstaining from actions does a person attain freedom from action, nor by renunciation alone does he reach perfection.
t.3.5: For no one can ever remain even for a moment without performing action; everyone is helplessly made to act by the guṇas born of prakṛti.
t.3.6: He who restrains the organs of action but sits dwelling in his mind on the objects of the senses, deluded in himself, is called a hypocrite.
t.3.7: But he who, restraining the senses with the mind, O Arjuna, undertakes the yoga of action with the organs of action, unattached, he excels.
t.3.8: Perform your prescribed action, for action is superior to inaction. Even the maintenance of your body would not be accomplished if you were inactive.
t.3.9: Except for action done for the sake of sacrifice, this world is bound by action. For that purpose, O Kaunteya, perform action, freed from attachment.
t.3.11: With this nourish the gods, and may those gods nourish you; nourishing one another, you will attain the highest good.
t.3.10: In ancient times Prajāpati, having created beings together with sacrifice, said: “By this you shall bring forth increase; let this be for you the wish-fulfilling cow that yields what you desire.”
t.3.12: For the gods, nourished by sacrifice, will give you the enjoyments you desire. He who enjoys what they have given without offering anything to them in return is truly a thief.
t.3.13: The good, who eat what remains of the sacrifice, are released from all sins; but the wicked, who cook only for their own sake, eat sin itself.
t.3.14: From food all beings come into existence, and food arises from rain. Rain comes from sacrifice, and sacrifice is born of action.
t.3.15: Know that action arises from Brahman, and Brahman arises from the Imperishable; therefore the all-pervading Brahman is ever established in sacrifice.
t.3.16: He who here does not follow the wheel thus set in motion, whose life is sin and who delights in the senses, lives in vain, O Pārtha.
t.3.17: But the man who delights in the Self alone, who is satisfied in the Self, and who is content in the Self alone, for him there is no work that must be done.
t.3.18: For him there is no purpose whatsoever here in what is done, nor in what is left undone; nor does he depend on any being among all beings for any purpose.
t.3.19: Therefore, always unattached, perform the work that must be done; for by performing action without attachment, a man attains the Supreme.
t.3.20: Indeed, it was through action alone that Janaka and others attained perfection. Even with a view to the welfare of the world, you ought to act.
t.3.21: Whatever the best person does, that very thing other people do as well. Whatever standard he sets, the world follows that.
t.3.22: O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that I must do, nor anything unattained that I need to attain; and yet I remain engaged in action.
t.3.24: If I were not to perform action, these worlds would perish; I would be the author of confusion, and I would destroy these creatures.
t.3.25: As the unwise act attached to action, O Bhārata, so should the wise act unattached, desiring to bring about the welfare of the world.
t.3.26: The wise one should not unsettle the understanding of the ignorant who are attached to action; rather, remaining disciplined and performing all actions himself, he should lead them to delight in all works.
t.3.28: But the knower of the truth, O mighty-armed one, concerning the two divisions of the guṇas and their actions, thinking, "The guṇas move among the guṇas," does not become attached.
t.3.23: For if I were ever to cease engaging in action, unwearied, O Pārtha, men would follow my path in every way.
t.3.29: Those who are deluded by the guṇas of prakṛti become attached to the actions of the guṇas. One who knows the whole should not unsettle those dull ones whose knowledge is incomplete.
t.3.30: Renouncing all actions in me, with your mind fixed on the supreme Self, free from desire and free from possessiveness, fight with your fever of anguish gone.
t.3.31: Those men who constantly follow this teaching of mine, full of faith and without carping, they too are released from the bonds of actions.
t.3.27: Actions are in every way performed by the qualities of nature, yet one whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, 'I am the one who will do them.'
t.3.32: But those who, finding fault with this teaching of mine, do not follow it, know them to be deluded in all knowledge, senseless, and lost.
t.3.33: Even a man of knowledge acts in accordance with his own nature. All beings follow their nature; what will restraint accomplish?
t.3.34: Attraction and aversion are seated in the object of each and every sense. One should not come under the sway of these two, for they are his adversaries.
t.3.35: Better is one's own dharma, though lacking in merit, than the dharma of another well performed. Death in one's own dharma is better; the dharma of another brings fear.
t.3.36: Arjuna said: Then by what is a man impelled to commit sin, O Vārṣṇeya, even against his own will, as if compelled by force?
t.3.37: The Blessed Lord said: It is desire, it is anger, born of the guṇa of rajas; all-devouring and most sinful, know this to be the enemy here.
t.3.38: As fire is covered by smoke, as a mirror by dust, and as an embryo is enveloped by the womb, so is this covered by that.
t.3.40: The senses, the mind and the intellect are said to be its seat; through these it veils knowledge and deludes the embodied one.
t.3.39: The wise have their knowledge veiled by this constant enemy, O Kaunteya, which takes the form of desire and is an insatiable fire.
t.3.41: Therefore, O bull among the Bharatas, first restraining the senses, cast off this sinful one, the destroyer of knowledge and realization.
t.3.42: They say that the senses are superior; higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect; but that which is beyond even the intellect is He.
t.3.43: Thus knowing that which is higher than the intellect, and steadying the self by the self, slay, O mighty-armed one, the enemy in the form of desire, so hard to overcome.
t.4.1: The Blessed Lord said: I declared this imperishable yoga to Vivasvān; Vivasvān told it to Manu, and Manu spoke it to Ikṣvāku.
t.4.2: Thus received through succession, this the royal sages knew. But that yoga, through a great lapse of time, has been lost here in this world, O scorcher of foes.
t.4.3: That very same ancient yoga has today been declared by me to you, since you are my devotee and my friend; for this is the supreme secret.
t.4.4: Arjuna said: Your birth was later, and the birth of Vivasvān was earlier. How am I to understand this, that you declared it in the beginning?
t.4.5: The Blessed Lord said: Many births of mine have passed away, and of yours too, Arjuna. I know them all, but you do not know them, O scorcher of foes.
t.4.6: Though I am unborn and my self is imperishable, though I am the Lord of all beings, yet, presiding over my own nature, I come into being through my own māyā.
t.4.7: Whenever there is a decline of dharma, O Bhārata, and a rise of adharma, then I send forth myself.
t.4.8: For the protection of the good and for the destruction of evildoers, for the sake of firmly establishing dharma, I come into being age after age.
t.4.9: He who thus knows in truth my divine birth and action, O Arjuna, does not go to rebirth on leaving the body; he comes to me.
t.4.10: Freed from passion, fear and anger, absorbed in me and taking refuge in me, many, purified by the austerity of knowledge, have attained my state of being.
t.4.11: In whatever way people approach me, in that very way I share myself with them. Everywhere, O Pārtha, people follow my path.
t.4.13: The fourfold order of society was created by me according to the division of qualities and actions. Though I am its maker, know me to be the non-doer, the imperishable.
t.4.12: Those longing for the success of their actions, worshipping the deities here, find that in the human world success born of action comes quickly indeed.
t.4.14: Actions do not stain me, nor do I have any longing for the fruit of action. One who knows me thus is not bound by actions.
t.4.15: Knowing this, even the ancient seekers of liberation performed action. Therefore you too must perform action, just as it was performed of old by the ancients.
t.4.16: What is action and what is inaction? Even the wise are bewildered about this. I shall explain to you that action, knowing which you will be freed from what is inauspicious.
t.4.17: One must indeed understand what action is, and one must understand what wrong action is, and one must understand what inaction is; deep and hard to fathom is the way of action.
t.4.18: One who sees inaction in action and action in inaction is wise among men; he is disciplined in yoga and a performer of all actions.
t.4.19: He whose every undertaking is free from desire and its motivating intent, whose actions have been burned up in the fire of knowledge, him the wise call a learned man.
t.4.20: Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever content and dependent on nothing, he does nothing at all, even though fully engaged in action.
t.4.21: Free from desire, with mind and self controlled, having abandoned all possessions, performing action with the body alone, he incurs no sin.
t.4.22: Content with whatever comes to him by chance, having passed beyond the pairs of opposites, free from envy, and even-minded in success and failure, he is not bound, even though he acts.
t.4.23: For one whose attachment is gone, who is liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge, and who performs action for the sake of sacrifice, the whole of his karma dissolves away completely.
t.4.24: The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman; Brahman alone is to be reached by him who is wholly absorbed in action that is Brahman.
t.4.25: Some yogins worship through sacrifice offered to the gods alone; others offer sacrifice itself, by means of sacrifice, into the fire of Brahman.
t.4.26: Some offer the senses, hearing and the rest, into the fires of restraint; others offer the objects of sense, sound and the rest, into the fires of the senses.
t.4.27: Others offer all the actions of the senses and the actions of the vital breath into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint, kindled by knowledge.
t.4.29: Others offer the prāṇa into the apāna, and likewise the apāna into the prāṇa; having restrained the courses of prāṇa and apāna, they are wholly devoted to prāṇāyāma.
t.4.28: Some offer their material possessions as sacrifice, others their austerity, and still others the practice of yoga; while ascetics of strict vows offer scriptural study and knowledge as their sacrifice.
t.4.30: Others, restraining their food, offer their life-breaths into the life-breaths. All of these are knowers of sacrifice, their impurities destroyed by sacrifice.
t.4.31: Those who eat the nectar that remains from sacrifice go to the eternal Brahman. This world is not for one who does not sacrifice; how then the other, O best of the Kurus?
t.4.32: Thus many kinds of sacrifices are spread out at the mouth of Brahman. Know them all to be born of action; knowing thus, you will be liberated.
t.4.33: Better than the sacrifice made of material things is the sacrifice of knowledge, O Paraṃtapa; all action without exception, O Pārtha, culminates in knowledge.
t.4.34: Know that by prostration, by thorough inquiry, and by service; the wise, the seers of truth, will instruct you in knowledge.
t.4.35: Knowing that, O Pāṇḍava, you will not again fall into delusion like this; and by that you will see all beings without exception in the Self, and then in me.
t.4.36: Even if you were the very worst of sinners, more sinful than all evildoers, you would cross over all wickedness by the raft of knowledge alone.
t.4.37: Just as a blazing fire reduces firewood to ashes, O Arjuna, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes.
t.4.38: Truly, nothing in this world is found that is as purifying as knowledge. One who is perfected in yoga finds that knowledge within himself, of his own accord, in the course of time.
t.4.39: The one who has faith, devoted to it and with senses restrained, attains knowledge; having attained knowledge, he quickly reaches supreme peace.
t.4.40: The ignorant one, the one without faith, and the one whose self is full of doubt perish. For the doubting soul there is neither this world nor the next, nor any happiness.
t.4.41: Actions do not bind one who has renounced actions through yoga, whose doubts have been cut asunder by knowledge, and who is self-possessed, O Dhanaṃjaya.
t.4.42: Therefore, having cut asunder with the sword of knowledge this doubt of the self, born of ignorance and lodged in the heart, take refuge in yoga and arise, O Bhārata!
t.5.1: Arjuna said: O Kṛṣṇa, you praise the renunciation of actions, and then again yoga. Tell me with certainty that one of these two which is the better.
t.5.2: The Blessed Lord said: Renunciation and the yoga of action both lead to the highest good; but of the two, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action.
t.5.3: He who neither hates nor desires should be known as one who is ever a renouncer; for, O mighty-armed one, free from the pairs of opposites, he is easily released from bondage.
t.5.4: It is the childish, not the wise, who speak of Sāṃkhya and Yoga as different. One who is properly established in even one of them obtains the fruit of both.
t.5.5: The state that is attained by the followers of Sāṃkhya is reached by the followers of Yoga as well. He who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one, he truly sees.
t.5.6: But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is hard to attain without yoga; the sage who is yoked in yoga attains Brahman before long.
t.5.7: One who is joined in yoga, pure in self, self-controlled and master of his senses, whose self has become the self of all beings, is not tainted even while acting.
t.5.8: "I do nothing at all," so should the one who is disciplined and knows the truth think, even while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, and breathing.
t.5.9: Even while speaking, letting go, grasping, opening and closing the eyes, he holds firmly that it is only the senses that are moving among the objects of the senses.
t.5.10: One who acts, placing all actions in Brahman and abandoning attachment, is not stained by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not stained by water.
t.5.11: With the body, with the mind, with the intellect, and even with the senses alone, yogins perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the purification of the self.
t.5.12: The disciplined man, having abandoned the fruit of action, attains lasting peace; the undisciplined man, attached to the fruit through the force of desire, is bound.
t.5.13: Having renounced all actions with the mind, the self-controlled embodied one dwells happily in the city of nine gates, neither acting at all nor causing action.
t.5.15: The all-pervading Lord does not take on anyone's sin, nor indeed anyone's good deed. Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; by that, living beings are deluded.
t.5.14: The Lord does not create agency for the world, nor actions, nor the union of action with its fruit; it is one's own nature that sets all this in motion.
t.5.16: But for those in whom that ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge of the Self, that knowledge, like the sun, illuminates the Supreme.
t.5.17: Those whose understanding is fixed on That, whose very self is That, whose steadfast devotion is to That, and who hold That as their supreme goal go to the state from which there is no return, their impurities shaken off by knowledge.
t.5.18: The wise see with an equal eye a brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and humility, a cow, an elephant, and even a dog and an outcaste who cooks dogs.
t.5.19: Even here in this world, creation is conquered by those whose mind is established in equality; for Brahman is flawless and equal, and therefore they are established in Brahman.
t.5.21: He whose self is unattached to external contacts finds the happiness that lies within the self; his self joined in the yoga of Brahman, he attains imperishable happiness.
t.5.20: One should not rejoice on obtaining what is pleasant, nor be troubled on meeting what is unpleasant; steady in understanding and free from delusion, the knower of Brahman abides in Brahman.
t.5.22: For the pleasures that are born of contact with the senses are indeed sources of sorrow; they have a beginning and an end, O Kaunteya, and the wise man does not delight in them.
t.5.23: He who is able, here in this very world, before release from the body, to withstand the surge born of desire and anger, he is a disciplined man, he is a happy man.
t.5.25: The seers whose sins are destroyed, whose doubts are cut asunder, who are self-controlled and who delight in the welfare of all beings, attain the nirvāṇa of Brahman.
t.5.26: For the ascetics who are freed from desire and anger, whose minds are controlled and who have known the Self, the extinction in Brahman exists all around them.
t.5.27: Shutting out external sense-contacts and fixing the gaze between the eyebrows, making equal the inward and outward breaths that move within the nostrils,
t.5.28: The sage whose senses, mind and intellect are controlled, who is wholly devoted to liberation, and from whom desire, fear and anger have departed, he is truly liberated forever.
t.5.29: Knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great lord of all the worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace.
t.5.24: He who is happy within, who rejoices within, and who likewise is illumined within, that yogī, having become one with Brahman, attains the nirvāṇa of Brahman.
t.6.1: The Blessed Lord said: He who performs the work that ought to be done, without depending on the fruit of action, is both a renunciant and a yogī; not he who is without the sacred fire, nor he who is without action.
t.6.2: What they call renunciation, know that to be yoga, O Pāṇḍava; for no one becomes a yogī who has not renounced his intentions.
t.6.3: For the sage who wishes to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means; for that same one, once he has ascended to yoga, tranquility is said to be the means.
t.6.4: For when one is attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions, and has renounced all intentions, then he is said to have ascended to yoga.
t.6.5: One should lift oneself up by oneself; one should not let oneself sink down. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.
t.6.6: For him by whom the self has been conquered by the self, the self is a friend of the self; but for one who has not conquered himself, the self would remain in enmity, just like an enemy.
t.6.7: For one who has conquered himself and is perfectly tranquil, the supreme Self remains steadfastly composed in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, and likewise in honor and dishonor.
t.6.8: The yogī whose self is content with knowledge and realized wisdom, who stands unshaken like an anvil, who has conquered his senses, and to whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are the same, is said to be truly established in yoga.
t.6.9: He who regards with an equal mind well-wishers, friends, enemies, the indifferent, the neutral, the hateful and kinsmen, and even the righteous and the sinful, excels.
t.6.10: The yogī should constantly discipline himself, remaining in seclusion, alone, with mind and self controlled, free from desire and without possessions.
t.6.12: There, having made the mind one-pointed, with the activities of thought and senses restrained, seated upon that seat, let him practise yoga for the purification of the self.
t.6.11: Having set up for himself a firm seat in a clean place, neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, deerskin and kuśa grass.
t.6.13: Holding the body, head and neck erect and motionless, remaining steady, gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking around in any direction.
t.6.15: Thus constantly disciplining himself, the yogī whose mind is controlled attains peace, the supreme nirvāṇa, which rests in me.
t.6.14: Serene in spirit and free from fear, steadfast in the vow of celibacy, having restrained the mind, with his thought fixed on me, he should sit disciplined, intent on me as the supreme goal.
t.6.16: Yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all, O Arjuna; nor for one who is given to too much sleep, nor indeed for one who stays always awake.
t.6.17: For one who is moderate in food and recreation, moderate in his efforts in actions, and moderate in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.
t.6.18: When the well-restrained mind rests in the Self alone, free from longing for all desires, then one is said to be established in yoga.
t.6.19: As a lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker, such is the simile remembered for the yogin of controlled mind who practices the yoga of the self.
t.6.20: That state in which the mind, restrained by the practice of yoga, comes to rest, and in which, seeing the Self by the self, one is content in the Self alone.
t.6.21: When he knows that supreme bliss which is grasped by the intellect and lies beyond the senses, and, established therein, never moves away from the truth;
t.6.22: Having gained that, one thinks no other gain greater than it; established in that, one is not shaken even by heavy sorrow.
t.6.23: One should know that which is called yoga to be the disconnection from union with sorrow. This yoga should be practiced with determination, with a mind free from despondency.
t.6.24: Having completely abandoned all desires born of mental intention, and having restrained the whole host of the senses on every side by the mind alone,
t.6.25: Little by little one should come to rest, with the intellect held firm by steadfastness; having made the mind abide in the Self, one should think of nothing at all.
t.6.26: From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away, from that very place he should restrain it and bring it under control in the Self alone.
t.6.27: Supreme happiness indeed comes to this yogin whose mind is perfectly tranquil, whose passion is stilled, who has become one with Brahman and is free from stain.
t.6.28: Thus constantly disciplining himself, the yogī, freed from impurity, easily attains the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman.
t.6.29: He whose self is joined in yoga, who sees the same everywhere, beholds the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self.
t.6.30: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me, to him I am never lost, and he is never lost to me.
t.6.31: The yogī who, established in oneness, worships me as dwelling in all beings, abides in me, however he may live.
t.6.32: He who, by comparison with himself, sees equality everywhere, O Arjuna, whether in pleasure or in pain, that yogī is considered the highest.
t.6.33: Arjuna said: This yoga of evenness which you have taught, O Madhusūdana, I do not see its steady foundation, because of restlessness.
t.6.34: For the mind is restless, Kṛṣṇa, turbulent, and exceedingly strong; I consider restraining it to be as very difficult as restraining the wind.
t.6.35: The Blessed Lord said: Without doubt, O mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and hard to restrain; but by practice, O son of Kuntī, and by dispassion, it is held in check.
t.6.36: Yoga is hard to attain for one whose self is unrestrained; this is my view. But by one whose self is under control and who strives, it can be attained through the proper means.
t.6.37: Arjuna said: One who is endowed with faith but lacks self-control, whose mind has strayed from yoga, and who has not attained perfection in yoga, what destination does he reach, O Kṛṣṇa?
t.6.38: O mighty-armed one, does he not, fallen from both, perish like a scattered cloud, without support and bewildered on the path of Brahman?
t.6.39: This doubt of mine, O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to cut away completely, for no one other than you can be found who could dispel this doubt.
t.6.40: The Blessed Lord said: O Pārtha, neither here nor in the world beyond is there destruction for him; for no one who does good, my dear friend, ever goes to an evil end.
t.6.41: Having attained the worlds of those who have done good deeds and having dwelt there for countless years, the one who has fallen from yoga is born in the house of the pure and the prosperous.
t.6.42: Or else he is born into a family of wise yogins; for a birth such as this is very hard to obtain in this world.
t.6.43: There he regains that union with the understanding he had in his former body, and from that point he strives once more toward perfection, O joy of the Kurus.
t.6.44: By that very former practice he is carried onward, even without his will. Even one who merely seeks to know yoga goes beyond the Veda, the Brahman of sound.
t.6.45: But the yogī who strives with diligent effort, cleansed of all sin and perfected through many births, then attains the supreme goal.
t.6.46: The yogī is superior to the ascetics, and he is considered superior even to the men of knowledge; the yogī is also superior to the men of ritual action. Therefore, Arjuna, be a yogī.
t.6.47: And of all yogins, the one who, full of faith, worships me with his inner self gone to me, he is considered by me to be the most devoted in yoga.
t.7.1: The Blessed Lord said: With your mind attached to me, O Pārtha, practicing yoga and taking refuge in me, hear how you will know me completely and without doubt.
t.7.2: I shall declare to you in full this knowledge together with realized understanding, knowing which nothing further remains here to be known.
t.7.3: Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection; and even among those who strive and have attained perfection, scarcely one knows me in truth.
t.7.4: Earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, and also the sense of I: thus is this nature of mine divided eightfold.
t.7.5: This is my lower nature; but know, O mighty-armed one, my other, higher nature, distinct from this, which has become the living being and by which this world is sustained.
t.7.6: Understand that all beings have these two natures as their womb. I am the origin of the whole world, and likewise its dissolution.
t.7.7: There is nothing whatsoever higher than me, O Dhanaṃjaya. All this is strung on me, like clusters of gems on a thread.
t.7.8: I am the taste in the waters, O Kaunteya, I am the radiance in the moon and the sun; I am the syllable Om in all the Vedas, the sound in the ether, and the manliness in men.
t.7.9: I am the pure fragrance in the earth and the brilliance in the fire; I am the life in all beings, and I am the austerity in the ascetics.
t.7.10: Know me, O Pārtha, to be the eternal seed of all beings. I am the intelligence of the intelligent, and I am the splendor of the splendid.
t.7.11: Of the strong, I am the strength that is free from desire and passion; in all beings I am the desire that is not contrary to dharma, O bull among the Bharatas.
t.7.12: And whatever states of being there are, whether sāttvika, rājasa, or tāmasa, know that they arise from Me alone; yet I am not in them, but they are in Me.
t.7.13: Deluded by these three states made of the guṇas, this whole world does not recognize Me, who am beyond them and imperishable.
t.7.14: For this divine māyā of mine, made of the guṇas, is hard to cross over. Those who take refuge in me alone cross beyond this māyā.
t.7.15: Evildoers, the deluded, the lowest of men, do not take refuge in me; their knowledge stolen away by māyā, they have resorted to a demonic nature.
t.7.16: Four kinds of virtuous people worship me, O Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom, O bull among the Bharatas.
t.7.18: All these are noble indeed, but the one who has knowledge is my very self; such is my view. For he, with a disciplined self, is established in me alone as the highest goal.
t.7.19: At the end of many births, the one possessed of knowledge takes refuge in me, realizing that Vāsudeva is all; such a great soul is very rare to find.
t.7.17: Of these, the man of knowledge, ever disciplined and devoted to the One alone, excels; for I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to me.
t.7.20: Those whose knowledge has been carried away by this or that desire resort to other deities, adopting this or that observance, constrained by their own nature.
t.7.21: Whatever form any devotee wishes to worship with faith, in each such person I make that very faith unwavering.
t.7.23: But the fruit of those of little understanding is finite. Worshippers of the gods go to the gods, while my devotees come to me.
t.7.22: Endowed with that faith, he strives to worship that form, and from it he obtains his desires, for those are in truth ordained by me alone.
t.7.24: The unintelligent think of Me, the unmanifest, as having come into manifestation, not knowing My supreme state, imperishable and unsurpassed.
t.7.25: Veiled by my yogamāyā, I am not manifest to all. This deluded world does not recognize me, the unborn and imperishable.
t.7.26: I know the beings that have passed away, those that are present, and those that are yet to come, O Arjuna, but no one knows Me.
t.7.27: O Bhārata, O scorcher of foes, through the delusion of the pairs of opposites, arising from desire and aversion, all beings fall into bewilderment at the time of creation.
t.7.28: But those people of virtuous deeds whose sin has come to an end, freed from the delusion of the pairs of opposites, worship me with firm resolve.
t.7.29: Those who, taking refuge in me, strive for liberation from old age and death know that Brahman, they know the whole of adhyātma, and karma in its entirety.
t.7.30: Those who know Me as the One who governs the elements and the gods, and as the Lord of sacrifice, they, with minds steadfastly united, know Me even at the time of departure from this life.
t.8.1: Arjuna said: What is that Brahman, what is the adhyātma, and what is karma, O Puruṣottama? And what is declared to be the adhibhūta, and what is called the adhidaiva?
t.8.2: Who is the adhiyajña here in this body, and how does he dwell in it, O Madhusūdana? And how are you to be known at the time of departure by those whose selves are controlled?
t.8.4: The perishable state of being is the adhibhūta, and the Puruṣa is the adhidaivata; I myself, here in this body, am the adhiyajña, O best of the embodied.
t.8.3: The Blessed Lord said: The supreme imperishable is Brahman; its own essential nature is called the inner Self. The creative outpouring that brings forth the existence of beings is known as karma.
t.8.5: And whoever, at the time of death, departs while remembering Me alone, having cast off the body, attains My state of being; of this there is no doubt.
t.8.6: Whatever state of being one remembers when at the end one gives up the body, to that very state one goes, O Kaunteya, having always been absorbed in that state of being.
t.8.7: Therefore, at all times remember me and fight. With mind and intellect offered to me, you will surely come to me alone; of this there is no doubt.
t.8.8: With a mind disciplined by the yoga of constant practice and straying to nothing else, O Pārtha, one who meditates without ceasing goes to the supreme, divine Puruṣa.
t.8.9: He who meditates upon the ancient Seer, the Ruler, subtler than the subtle, the Sustainer of all, whose form is beyond thought, radiant like the sun and beyond all darkness.
t.8.10: At the time of departure, with an unmoving mind, endowed with devotion and with the strength of yoga, having made the vital breath enter fully between the brows, he reaches that supreme, divine Puruṣa.
t.8.11: That which the knowers of the Veda call the Imperishable, which ascetics free from passion enter, and desiring which they practise celibacy, that state I shall declare to you in brief.
t.8.12: Restraining all the gates of the body and confining the mind within the heart, placing his own life-breath in the head, he is established in the concentration of yoga.
t.8.13: He who has uttered Om, the one-syllabled Brahman, and departs while remembering me as he abandons the body, attains the supreme goal.
t.8.14: He who, with a mind turned to nothing else, constantly remembers me day after day, for that yogin, ever disciplined, I am easily attained, O Pārtha.
t.8.15: Having come to me, the great-souled ones, who have attained the highest perfection, do not again obtain birth, that impermanent abode of sorrow.
t.8.16: The worlds, up to the realm of Brahmā, are those of one who must return again, O Arjuna; but having reached me, O son of Kuntī, there is no rebirth.
t.8.17: Those people who know day and night know that a day of Brahmā extends to a thousand yugas, and that his night likewise ends only after a thousand yugas.
t.8.18: At the coming of the day, all manifest things arise from the unmanifest; at the coming of the night, they dissolve into that very thing which is called the unmanifest.
t.8.19: This very same multitude of beings, coming into being again and again, is dissolved helplessly at the coming of night, O Pārtha, and comes forth again at the coming of day.
t.8.20: But beyond that unmanifest there is another existence, unmanifest and eternal, which does not perish when all beings perish.
t.8.21: That Unmanifest is called the Imperishable; they declare it to be the supreme goal. Having attained it, they do not return; that is my supreme abode.
t.8.22: That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, within whom all beings abide and by whom all this is pervaded, is attainable only through undivided devotion.
t.8.23: But the time at which yogins, having departed, go to non-return and also to return, that time I shall declare to you, O bull among the Bharatas.
t.8.24: Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern course of the sun: departing then, people who know Brahman go to Brahman.
t.8.25: Smoke, night, and likewise the dark fortnight, the six months of the sun's southern course: there the yogī, having attained the lunar light, returns.
t.8.26: These two paths of the world, the bright and the dark, are indeed held to be eternal. By the one, a person goes to non-return; by the other, he returns again.
t.8.27: Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogī is ever deluded. Therefore, at all times, be steadfast in yoga, O Arjuna.
t.8.28: Whatever fruit of merit is declared for the Vedas, for sacrifices, for austerities and for gifts, the yogī who knows this goes beyond all of it and attains the supreme, primeval abode.
t.9.1: The Blessed Lord said: But to you, who are free from envy, I shall declare this most secret knowledge together with realization, knowing which you will be freed from evil.
t.9.2: This is the king of knowledge, the king of secrets, the supreme purifier; it is directly perceived, in accord with dharma, very easy to practice, and imperishable.
t.9.3: Those people who have no faith in this dharma, O scorcher of foes, do not attain me and return to the path of death and saṃsāra.
t.9.4: By me, in my unmanifest form, this entire universe is pervaded. All beings abide in me, but I do not abide in them.
t.9.5: And yet beings do not dwell in me: behold my sovereign yoga! Sustaining beings yet not dwelling in beings, my Self brings beings into existence.
t.9.6: Just as the mighty wind, moving everywhere, always rests in space, so too all beings rest in me; understand it thus.
t.9.7: All beings, O Kaunteya, pass into my own Prakṛti at the end of a kalpa; at the beginning of a kalpa I send them forth again.
t.9.8: Taking hold of my own Prakṛti, I send forth again and again this entire multitude of beings, helpless under the sway of Prakṛti.
t.9.9: And these actions do not bind me, O Dhanaṃjaya, for I sit as one indifferent, unattached to those actions.
t.9.11: Fools disregard me when I have taken on a human body, not knowing my supreme nature as the great lord of beings.
t.9.10: Through me as overseer, prakṛti, the whole of what moves and what does not move, is brought forth. For this reason, O Kaunteya, the world revolves.
t.9.12: Vain in their hopes, vain in their actions, vain in their knowledge and devoid of discernment, they take refuge in the deluding nature of rākṣasas and asuras.
t.9.13: But the great-souled ones, O Pārtha, taking refuge in the divine nature, worship me with minds turned to nothing else, knowing me as the imperishable origin of beings.
t.9.14: Always glorifying Me, striving, firm in their vows, and bowing down to Me with devotion, ever steadfast, they worship Me.
t.9.15: And others, too, sacrificing with the sacrifice of knowledge, worship me, who face in every direction, as one, as distinct, and in many ways.
t.9.16: I am the ritual, I am the sacrifice, I am the offering to the ancestors, I am the healing herb; I am the mantra, I indeed am the clarified butter, I am the fire, and I am the act of offering.
t.9.17: I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer, and the grandfather; I am what is to be known, the purifier, the syllable Oṃ, and also the Ṛc, the Sāman, and the Yajus.
t.9.22: Those people who, thinking of no other, meditate on me and worship me, to them, ever devoted, I bring the attainment of what they lack and the preservation of what they have.
t.9.18: I am the goal, the sustainer, the lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge and the friend; I am the origin and the dissolution, the ground, the treasure-house, and the imperishable seed.
t.9.21: Having enjoyed that vast world of heaven, they enter the world of mortals when their merit is exhausted. Thus, following the dharma of the three Vedas and desiring objects of desire, they obtain going and coming.
t.9.20: Those who know the three Vedas, drinkers of soma, cleansed of sin, having worshipped me with sacrifices, pray for the way to heaven. Reaching the holy world of Indra, lord of the gods, they enjoy in heaven the divine pleasures of the gods.
t.9.19: I give heat; I withhold the rain and send it forth. I am immortality and also death, being and non-being, O Arjuna.
t.9.23: Even those devotees who, endowed with faith, worship other deities, they too worship Me alone, O Kaunteya, though not according to the prescribed rule.
t.9.24: For I alone am the enjoyer and also the lord of all sacrifices; but they do not know Me in truth, and therefore they fall.
t.9.25: Those devoted to the gods go to the gods; those devoted to the ancestors go to the ancestors; those who worship the spirits go to the spirits; and those who sacrifice to me come to me.
t.9.26: Whoever offers to me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, that offering of devotion I accept from the one whose self is pure.
t.9.27: Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, whatever austerity you practise, O Kaunteya, do that as an offering to me.
t.9.28: Thus you will be freed from the bonds of action, which bear good and evil fruits; with your self disciplined by the yoga of renunciation, liberated, you will come to me.
t.9.29: I am the same toward all beings; none is hateful to me, and none is dear. But those who worship me with devotion are in me, and I too am in them.
t.9.30: Even if one of very wicked conduct worships me with undivided devotion, he must be regarded as righteous indeed, for he has rightly resolved.
t.9.31: Swiftly he becomes righteous in soul and attains lasting peace. O Kaunteya, know this for certain: my devotee never perishes.
t.9.32: For, O Pārtha, even those who may be of sinful birth, women, vaiśya women, and likewise śūdras, they too, taking refuge in me, attain the supreme goal.
t.9.33: How much more, then, the holy brāhmaṇas and the devoted royal sages! Having come into this transient and joyless world, worship Me.
t.9.34: Fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, sacrifice to me, and bow down to me. Having thus disciplined yourself, with me as your supreme goal, you will come to me alone.
t.10.1: The Blessed Lord said: Once again, O mighty-armed one, hear my supreme word, which I shall speak to you, who take delight in it, out of a wish for your welfare.
t.10.2: Neither the hosts of gods nor the great sages know my origin, for I am in every way the source of the gods and of the great sages.
t.10.3: He who knows me as unborn and without beginning, the great Lord of the worlds, he among mortals is undeluded and is freed from all sins.
t.10.4: Intelligence, knowledge, freedom from delusion, forbearance, truthfulness, self-restraint and tranquility, pleasure and pain, birth and non-existence, fear and also fearlessness,
t.10.5: Non-violence, equanimity, contentment, austerity, charity, fame and infamy: these various states of beings arise from me alone.
t.10.7: He who truly knows this manifold glory and this yoga of mine is united with unwavering yoga; of this there is no doubt.
t.10.6: The seven great sages of old, and likewise the four Manus, sharing my nature, were born from my mind, and from them have come these creatures in the world.
t.10.8: I am the origin of all; from me everything proceeds. Understanding this, the wise, filled with devotion, worship me.
t.10.9: With their minds fixed on Me, their lives devoted to Me, enlightening one another and constantly speaking of Me, they are content and they rejoice.
t.10.10: To those who are ever devoted and worship Me with love, I give that yoga of understanding by which they come to Me.
t.10.11: Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their very being, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge.
t.10.12: Arjuna said: You are the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the supreme purifier; you are the one they proclaim as the eternal divine Person, the primal God, unborn and all-pervading.
t.10.13: All the seers have declared this of you, and so has the divine seer Nārada, as well as Asita, Devala and Vyāsa; and you yourself tell me so.
t.10.14: All this that you tell me, O Keśava, I hold to be true. For neither the gods nor the Dānavas know your manifestation, O Blessed Lord.
t.10.16: You ought to describe completely your own divine manifestations, the manifestations by which you pervade these worlds and abide.
t.10.15: You yourself alone know yourself through yourself, O Supreme Person, O source of beings, O lord of beings, O god of gods, O lord of the world.
t.10.17: How may I know you, O Yogin, while constantly meditating upon you? And in what various states of being are you to be contemplated by me, O Bhagavan?
t.10.18: Tell me again in detail, O Janārdana, of your yoga and your divine manifestations, for as I listen to this nectar, I am never satisfied.
t.10.19: The Blessed Lord said: Very well, I shall tell you of My divine self-manifestations, O best of the Kurus, but only the principal ones, for there is no end to My extent.
t.10.20: I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, abiding in the heart of all beings. I am the beginning, the middle, and also the very end of beings.
t.10.21: Of the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu; of lights I am the radiant sun. Of the Maruts I am Marīci; among the stars I am the moon.
t.10.22: Of the Vedas I am the Sāmaveda; of the gods I am Vāsava; of the senses I am the mind; and of living beings I am consciousness.
t.10.23: Among the Rudras I am Śaṃkara, and among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas I am Vitteśa, the lord of wealth. Among the Vasus I am Pāvaka, and among the peaked mountains I am Meru.
t.10.24: Know me, O Pārtha, as Bṛhaspati, the chief among the household priests; among army leaders I am Skanda, and among bodies of water I am the ocean.
t.10.25: Among the great sages I am Bhṛgu; among utterances I am the single syllable. Among sacrifices I am the sacrifice of japa, and among immovable things I am the Himālaya.
t.10.26: Among all trees I am the Aśvattha, and among the divine sages I am Nārada; among the Gandharvas I am Citraratha, and among the perfected ones I am the sage Kapila.
t.10.27: Among horses, know me to be Uccaiḥśravas, born of the nectar of immortality; among lordly elephants, Airāvata; and among men, the king.
t.10.28: Among weapons I am the thunderbolt, among cows I am Kāmadhuk, the wish-fulfilling cow; of progenitors I am Kandarpa, and among serpents I am Vāsuki.
t.10.29: Of the Nāgas I am Ananta, and of the water-dwellers I am Varuṇa; of the ancestors I am Aryaman, and of those who restrain I am Yama.
t.10.30: Among the Daityas I am Prahlāda, and among those who reckon I am Time; among beasts I am the lord of beasts, and among birds I am Vainateya.
t.10.31: Of purifiers I am the wind; of the wielders of weapons I am Rāma. Of fishes I am the makara, and of rivers I am the Jāhnavī.
t.10.32: Of creations I am the beginning and the end, and also the middle, O Arjuna; of sciences I am the science of the Self, and of those who debate I am the reasoned discourse.
t.10.33: Of letters I am the letter A, and of compounds I am the dvaṃdva. I alone am imperishable Time; I am the Sustainer, facing in all directions.
t.10.34: I am all-devouring Death, and I am the origin of all that is yet to be. Among feminine things, I am fame, prosperity, speech, memory, intelligence, steadfastness and forgiveness.
t.10.35: Likewise, of the Sāman hymns I am the Bṛhatsāman; of the metres I am the Gāyatrī. Of the months I am Mārgaśīrṣa; of the seasons I am the flower-bearing spring.
t.10.36: Of those who deceive, I am the gambling; I am the splendor of the splendid. I am victory, I am resolve, I am the goodness of the good.
t.10.37: Of the Vṛṣṇis I am Vāsudeva; of the Pāṇḍavas, Dhanaṃjaya; of the sages I am Vyāsa; and of the seers, the seer Uśanas.
t.10.40: There is no end to my divine manifestations, O scorcher of foes. But this extent of my glory has been declared by me only by way of example.
t.10.38: Of those who subdue, I am the rod of punishment; of those who seek victory, I am statecraft. Of secret things I am silence, and of the wise I am wisdom.
t.10.41: Whatever being there is that is endowed with glory, splendid, or mighty, know that very thing to have sprung from a portion of my radiance.
t.10.42: But what need is there for you, Arjuna, to know all this in such detail? I stand, supporting this entire universe with a single fraction of Myself.
t.10.39: And whatever is the seed of all beings, that am I, O Arjuna; there is no being, moving or unmoving, that could exist without me.
t.11.1: Arjuna said: By the supreme and secret word concerning the Self that you have spoken out of kindness to me, this delusion of mine has gone away.
t.11.2: For I have heard from you in detail, O lotus-eyed one, of the origin and dissolution of beings, and also of your imperishable greatness.
t.11.3: O Supreme Lord, it is just as you have described yourself. Yet I wish to see your divine, sovereign form, O Supreme Person.
t.11.4: O Lord, if you think that it can be seen by me, then, O Lord of Yoga, show me your imperishable Self.
t.11.5: The Blessed Lord said: Behold, O Pārtha, my forms by hundreds and by thousands, manifold and divine, of various colors and shapes.
t.11.6: Behold the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and likewise the Maruts; behold, O Bhārata, many wonders never seen before.
t.11.7: Behold now, O Guḍākeśa, the entire universe, with all that moves and does not move, standing here as one in my body, and whatever else you wish to see.
t.11.8: But you cannot see me with these eyes of your own. I give you divine sight; behold my sovereign yoga.
t.11.9: Saṃjaya said: Having spoken thus, O King, Hari, the great Lord of Yoga, then revealed to Pārtha his supreme, sovereign form.
t.11.10: A form with many mouths and eyes, presenting many wondrous sights, adorned with many divine ornaments, and holding many divine weapons raised aloft.
t.11.12: If the radiance of a thousand suns were to blaze forth all at once in the sky, that might resemble the radiance of that great-souled one.
t.11.11: Wearing celestial garlands and garments, anointed with divine fragrances, the God composed of all wonders, infinite, with faces turned in every direction.
t.11.13: There, in the body of the God of gods, the son of Pāṇḍu then beheld the entire universe, divided in many ways, gathered together in one place.
t.11.14: Then Dhanaṃjaya, filled with wonder, his hair standing on end, bowed his head to the god and, with joined palms, spoke.
t.11.16: I see You, of endless form on every side, with many arms, bellies, mouths and eyes. O Lord of the universe, O You whose form is the universe, I see no end of You, no middle, and again no beginning.
t.11.15: Arjuna said: O God, in your body I see all the gods and likewise the hosts of the various kinds of beings: Brahmā the lord seated on his lotus throne, all the sages, and the divine serpents.
t.11.17: I see You, crowned, bearing the mace and the discus, a mass of splendor blazing on every side, hard to behold all around, radiant like the burning fire and the sun, immeasurable.
t.11.18: You are the Imperishable, the Supreme, the one to be known; you are the supreme resting place of this universe. You are the unchanging guardian of eternal dharma; you are the everlasting Puruṣa, so I believe.
t.11.19: I see You without beginning, middle, or end, of infinite power, with countless arms, the moon and sun as Your eyes, Your mouth a blazing fire, scorching this whole universe with Your own radiance.
t.11.20: This space between heaven and earth, and all the directions, are pervaded by you alone. Seeing this wondrous and terrible form of yours, the three worlds tremble, O great-souled one.
t.11.21: These hosts of gods enter into you; some, afraid, praise you with joined palms. Saying "May it be well!", the hosts of great seers and Siddhas praise you with abundant hymns.
t.11.22: The Rudras, Ādityas and Vasus, and those who are the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, the Maruts and the Ūṣmapas, and the hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras and Siddhas all gaze upon you, utterly amazed.
t.11.23: Seeing your immense form, O mighty-armed one, with many mouths and eyes, with many arms, thighs and feet, with many bellies, terrible with many tusks, the worlds are shaken, and so am I.
t.11.24: Seeing you touching the sky, blazing, of many colors, with mouths wide open and vast flaming eyes, my inmost self is shaken with fear, and I find neither steadiness nor peace, O Viṣṇu.
t.11.25: Having merely seen your mouths, terrible with tusks and resembling the fire of time's end, I know not the directions and find no refuge; be gracious, Lord of the gods, abode of the world!
t.11.27: Rushing, they enter your fearsome mouths, terrible with tusks; some are seen caught between your teeth, their heads crushed to powder.
t.11.26: And all these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with the hosts of the rulers of the earth, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and likewise that son of the charioteer, along with the foremost warriors of our own side as well, are rushing toward you.
t.11.28: As the many torrents of the rivers rush headlong toward the ocean alone, so do these heroes of the world of men enter your mouths, blazing all around.
t.11.29: As moths rush with swift speed into a blazing fire to their destruction, so too do the worlds rush with swift speed into your mouths to their destruction.
t.11.30: Devouring all the worlds on every side with your flaming mouths, you lick them up again and again; filling the whole universe with brilliance, your fierce rays blaze forth and scorch it, O Viṣṇu.
t.11.31: Tell me who you are, you of terrible form; salutation be to you, O best of gods, be gracious! I wish to know you, the primal one, for I do not understand your course of action.
t.11.32: The Blessed Lord said: I am Time, the mighty destroyer of the worlds, set forth here to annihilate the worlds. Even without you, all these warriors arrayed in the opposing ranks shall cease to be.
t.11.33: Therefore stand up and win glory; having conquered your enemies, enjoy a prosperous kingdom. By me alone these have already been slain; be merely the instrument, O Savyasācin.
t.11.34: Droṇa and Bhīṣma and Jayadratha and Karṇa, and likewise the other heroic warriors, already slain by me, do you slay; do not be distressed. Fight, and you will conquer your rivals in battle.
t.11.35: Sañjaya said: Having heard these words of Keśava, the crowned one, trembling, with joined palms, made obeisance, and bowing down again, utterly terrified, spoke to Kṛṣṇa in a faltering voice.
t.11.36: Arjuna said: Rightly, O Hṛṣīkeśa, does the world rejoice and delight in your praise; the terrified Rākṣasas flee in all directions, and all the hosts of the Siddhas bow down to you.
t.11.37: And why should they not bow down to you, O Great Soul, who are greater even than Brahmā, to you, the original creator? O Infinite One, Lord of the gods, Abode of the universe, you are the imperishable, being and non-being, and that which is beyond both.
t.11.39: You are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, the moon, Prajāpati, and the great-grandfather. Salutations, salutations to You a thousand times, and again and yet again, salutations, salutations to You!
t.11.38: You are the primal God, the ancient Person; you are the supreme resting place of this universe. You are the knower of what is to be known and of the supreme abode; by you this universe is pervaded, O you of infinite form.
t.11.40: Salutation to you in front and also behind; let salutation be to you on every side, O All! You are of infinite valor and immeasurable might; you pervade all, and therefore you are all.
t.11.42: And if, for the sake of jest, you were treated with disrespect while at play, resting, sitting, or eating, whether alone or in the presence of others, O Acyuta, for that I beg forgiveness of you, the immeasurable one.
t.11.41: Whatever I have said rashly, thinking of you as a friend, calling out 'O Kṛṣṇa, O Yādava, O friend,' not knowing this greatness of yours, whether out of carelessness or even out of affection...
t.11.43: You are the father of this world, of all that moves and does not move; you are its object of worship and its most venerable teacher. There is none equal to you; how then could there be another greater than you, even in the three worlds, O you of incomparable power?
t.11.44: Therefore, bowing down and prostrating my body, I seek your grace, O Lord worthy of praise. As a father bears with his son, as a friend with his friend, as a lover with the beloved, so you should bear with me, O God.
t.11.46: I wish to see you just as before, wearing a crown, bearing a mace, with the discus in hand. O thousand-armed one, O you whose form is the universe, become that very four-armed form.
t.11.47: The Blessed Lord said: Arjuna, out of my grace I have, by my own yogic power, shown you this supreme form, radiant, universal, infinite and primal, this form of mine that no one other than you has ever seen before.
t.11.45: Having seen what was never seen before, I am thrilled, and yet my mind is shaken with fear. Show me, O God, that very form of yours; be gracious, O Lord of the gods, O abode of the universe!
t.11.48: Neither by the Vedas, sacrifices and study, nor by gifts, nor by rituals, nor by severe austerities can I in this form be seen in the world of men by anyone other than you, O great hero of the Kurus.
t.11.49: Let there be no distress for you, nor a state of bewilderment, at having seen this terrible form of mine. Free from fear and with a gladdened mind, behold once again that very form of mine.
t.11.50: Saṃjaya said: Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva again revealed his own form; and the great-souled one, becoming once more gentle in form, consoled him who was terrified.
t.11.51: Arjuna said: Seeing this gentle human form of yours, O Janārdana, I have now become composed in mind and have returned to my normal nature.
t.11.52: The Blessed Lord said: This form of mine that you have seen is very hard to behold; even the gods are ever longing for a sight of this form.
t.11.53: Not by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be seen in this form, as you have seen me.
t.11.54: But only by undivided devotion, O Arjuna, can I in this form be known, and truly seen, and entered into, O scorcher of foes.
t.11.55: He who does work for me, who holds me as the supreme goal, who is devoted to me, free from attachment, and without enmity toward any being, he comes to me, O Pāṇḍava.
t.12.1: Arjuna said: Those devotees who, ever steadfast in this way, worship you, and those who worship the imperishable, the unmanifest, which of them are the best knowers of yoga?
t.12.2: The Blessed Lord said: Those who, having fixed their mind on Me, worship Me, ever steadfast and endowed with supreme faith, are considered by Me to be the most perfectly united in yoga.
t.12.3: But those who worship the imperishable, the indefinable, the unmanifest, the all-pervading and unthinkable, the unchanging, the immovable, the eternal…
t.12.4: Having fully restrained the whole host of the senses, even-minded in every circumstance, and delighting in the welfare of all beings, they attain to me alone.
t.12.5: Greater is the toil of those whose minds are attached to the unmanifest, for the unmanifest goal is attained with difficulty by embodied beings.
t.12.6: But those who, having renounced all actions in me and holding me as the supreme goal, worship me, meditating on me with undivided devotion,
t.12.7: For those whose minds are absorbed in me, O Pārtha, I soon become the deliverer from the ocean of death and saṃsāra.
t.12.8: Fix your mind on me alone, and let your understanding enter into me. Thereafter you will dwell in me alone; of this there is no doubt.
t.12.9: If, however, you are unable to fix your mind steadily on me, then, O Dhanaṃjaya, seek to attain me through the yoga of practice.
t.12.11: If you are unable to do even this, then, taking refuge in my yoga and with self restrained, give up the fruits of all actions.
t.12.12: Better indeed is knowledge than practice; meditation is superior to knowledge; renunciation of the fruits of action is better than meditation, and from renunciation comes peace immediately.
t.12.13: He who bears no hatred toward any being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from possessiveness and from ego, the same in sorrow and in joy, and forgiving,
t.12.14: The yogī who is ever content, self-controlled and firm in resolve, whose mind and intellect are offered to me, who is devoted to me, he is dear to me.
t.12.15: He from whom the world does not shrink in agitation, and who does not shrink in agitation from the world, who is free from elation, impatience, fear, and anxiety, he too is dear to me.
t.12.16: He who is free from expectation, pure, skillful, unconcerned, and rid of distress, who has renounced all undertakings, he who is devoted to me is dear to me.
t.12.17: He who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires, who has renounced both the auspicious and the inauspicious, and who is full of devotion, he is dear to me.
t.12.10: If you are unable even to practice, be intent on work for my sake; even performing actions for my sake, you will attain perfection.
t.12.18: He who is the same toward foe and friend, and likewise in honor and dishonor, who is the same in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, and is free from attachment.
t.12.19: The man who is the same in blame and praise, silent, content with whatever comes, homeless, steady in mind, and full of devotion is dear to me.
t.12.20: But those who, full of faith and holding me as their highest goal, devotedly honor this righteous nectar of immortality just as it has been declared, those devotees are exceedingly dear to me.
t.13.1: Arjuna said: Prakṛti and Puruṣa, the field and the knower of the field, knowledge and that which is to be known, these I wish to learn, O Keśava.
t.13.2: The Blessed Lord said: This body, O Kaunteya, is called the field; the one who knows it is called the knower of the field by those who know of these things.
t.13.3: And know Me also as the knower of the field in all fields, O Bhārata. The knowledge of the field and the knower of the field, that is knowledge in My view.
t.13.4: Hear from me in brief what that field is, of what nature it is, what its modifications are, and from what it arises; and who he is and what his powers are.
t.13.5: It has been sung by the seers in many ways, distinctly in various hymns, and also in the words of the Brahmasūtras, well reasoned and conclusive.
t.13.6: The great elements, the ego-sense, the intellect and the unmanifest too, the ten senses and the one, and the five objects of the senses.
