t.13.8: Absence of pride, absence of hypocrisy, non-violence, patience, uprightness, service of the teacher, purity, steadfastness, and self-restraint.
t.13.7: Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, consciousness and steadfastness: this, in brief, is declared to be the field together with its modifications.
t.13.9: Dispassion toward the objects of the senses, and also absence of egoism; constant perception of the evil and suffering in birth, death, old age, and disease.
t.13.10: Non-attachment, freedom from clinging to son, wife, home and the like, and constant evenness of mind amid the arrival of the desired and the undesired.
t.13.11: Unswerving devotion to me through the discipline of exclusive union, resort to solitary places, and distaste for the crowds of men.
t.13.12: Constancy in the knowledge of the Self and insight into the purpose of the knowledge of truth: this is declared to be knowledge, and whatever is contrary to it is ignorance.
t.13.13: I shall declare that which is to be known, knowing which one attains immortality: the beginningless supreme Brahman, which is said to be neither being nor non-being.
t.13.14: With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads and mouths on every side, hearing everywhere, That abides in the world, enveloping all.
t.13.15: It shines through the qualities of all the senses, yet is devoid of all the senses; unattached, it nonetheless sustains all; free of the guṇas, it is yet the enjoyer of the guṇas.
t.13.16: It is outside and inside all beings, both unmoving and moving. Because of its subtlety it cannot be known; it is far away, and yet it is near.
t.13.17: Undivided, yet it abides among beings as if divided; that which is to be known is the sustainer of beings, their devourer, and their creator.
t.13.19: Thus the field, as well as knowledge and that which is to be known, have been briefly described. My devotee, having understood this, attains to My state of being.
t.13.18: It is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and that which is to be reached through knowledge; it is seated in the heart of all.
t.13.20: Know that prakṛti and puruṣa are both without beginning, and know also that the modifications and the guṇas are born of prakṛti.
t.13.21: Prakṛti is said to be the cause in the agency of effect and instrument; Puruṣa is said to be the cause in the experiencing of pleasures and pains.
t.13.22: For the puruṣa, abiding in prakṛti, experiences the guṇas born of prakṛti; attachment to the guṇas is the cause of its births in good and evil wombs.
t.13.23: The supreme Puruṣa in this body is the witness and the one who consents, the sustainer, the enjoyer, the great Lord, and is also called the Supreme Self.
t.13.24: He who thus knows the Puruṣa and Prakṛti together with the guṇas, though he may be living in any way whatsoever, is not born again.
t.13.25: Some, through meditation, behold the Self in the self by the self; others by the yoga of Sāṃkhya, and still others by the yoga of action.
t.13.27: Whatever being comes into existence, whether unmoving or moving, know that it arises from the union of the field and the knower of the field, O bull among the Bharatas.
t.13.26: But others, not knowing in this way, worship after hearing from others; and they too, devoted to what they have heard, surely pass beyond death.
t.13.28: He who sees the Supreme Lord abiding equally in all beings, the imperishable within the perishing, truly sees.
t.13.29: For seeing the Lord as equally present everywhere, he does not harm the self by the self; thereupon he goes to the supreme goal.
t.13.30: He who sees that all actions are performed in every way by Prakṛti alone, and likewise sees the Self as the non-doer, he truly sees.
t.13.31: When he sees the separate existence of beings as resting in the One, and their expansion from that alone, then he attains Brahman.
t.13.32: Because it is without beginning and without qualities, this imperishable Supreme Self, though dwelling in the body, O Kaunteya, neither acts nor is tainted.
t.13.33: Just as the all-pervading ether, because of its subtlety, is not tainted, so the Self, though present everywhere in the body, is not tainted.
t.13.34: Just as the one sun illumines this entire world, so does the lord of the field illumine the entire field, O Bhārata.
t.13.35: Those who, with the eye of knowledge, thus know the difference between the field and the knower of the field, and the liberation of beings from Prakṛti, go to the Supreme.
t.14.1: The Blessed Lord said: I shall declare once more that supreme knowledge, the highest of all knowledges, having known which all the sages have gone from here to the supreme perfection.
t.14.2: Having taken refuge in this knowledge, those who have attained a nature like mine are not born even at the time of creation, nor are they troubled at the time of dissolution.
t.14.3: My womb is the great Brahman; in it I place the seed. From that, O Bhārata, comes the birth of all beings.
t.14.4: O son of Kuntī, whatever forms come into being in all wombs, the great Brahman is their womb, and I am the seed-giving father.
t.14.5: Sattva, rajas and tamas, these guṇas born of prakṛti, bind fast in the body the imperishable embodied one, O mighty-armed one.
t.14.6: Of these, sattva, being stainless, is luminous and free from disease; it binds by attachment to happiness and by attachment to knowledge, O sinless one.
t.14.7: Know rajas to be of the nature of passion, arising from craving and attachment; it binds the embodied one, O Kaunteya, through attachment to action.
t.14.8: But know tamas to be born of ignorance, deluding all embodied beings; it binds them, O Bhārata, through heedlessness, sloth, and sleep.
t.14.9: Sattva binds one to happiness, rajas to action, O Bhārata; but tamas, veiling knowledge, binds one to heedlessness.
t.14.11: When the light of knowledge arises in all the gates of this body, then one should know that sattva has increased.
t.14.10: Overpowering rajas and tamas, sattva prevails, O Bhārata; tamas likewise prevails by overpowering rajas and sattva, and in the same way rajas prevails by overpowering tamas and sattva.
t.14.12: Greed, activity, the undertaking of actions, restlessness, and longing: these arise when rajas has increased, O bull among the Bharatas.
t.14.13: Darkness, inertia, heedlessness and delusion: these arise when tamas has increased, O delight of the Kurus.
t.14.14: But when the embodied one meets dissolution while sattva is predominant, he then attains the pure worlds of those who know the highest.
t.14.15: Meeting death in rajas, one is born among those attached to action; likewise, dying in tamas, one is born in the wombs of the deluded.
t.14.16: They say that the fruit of a well-performed action is sāttvika and spotless, but the fruit of rajas is sorrow, and the fruit of tamas is ignorance.
t.14.17: From sattva knowledge is born, and from rajas greed indeed; from tamas arise heedlessness and delusion, and ignorance as well.
t.14.18: Those established in sattva go upward; the rājasic remain in the middle; the tāmasic, abiding in the conduct of the lowest guṇa, go downward.
t.14.19: When the seer perceives no agent other than the guṇas, and knows that which is beyond the guṇas, he attains to my state of being.
t.14.20: Having gone beyond these three guṇas, which arise from the body, the embodied one, freed from birth, death, old age and sorrow, attains immortality.
t.14.21: Arjuna said: By what marks is one known who has gone beyond these three guṇas, O Lord? What is his conduct, and how does he pass beyond these three guṇas?
t.14.22: The Blessed Lord said: O Pāṇḍava, he who does not hate illumination, activity, and delusion when they have arisen, nor longs for them when they have ceased.
t.14.23: He who, seated as one indifferent, is not shaken by the guṇas, who, knowing that it is only the guṇas that are acting, stands firm and does not waver.
t.14.24: He who is the same in sorrow and in joy, who abides in his own self, to whom a clod of earth, a stone and gold are alike, who regards the pleasant and the unpleasant as equal, who is steadfast, and to whom blame and praise of himself are the same.
t.14.25: He who is the same in honor and dishonor, the same toward the side of friend and of foe, and who has abandoned all undertakings, is said to have transcended the guṇas.
t.14.26: And he who serves me with the unwavering yoga of devotion, having gone beyond these guṇas, becomes fit for becoming Brahman.
t.14.27: For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the immortal and imperishable, of eternal dharma, and of absolute bliss.
t.15.1: The Blessed Lord said: They speak of the imperishable aśvattha tree with its roots above and its branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns; he who knows it is a knower of the Vedas.
t.15.2: Below and above spread its branches, nourished by the guṇas, with sense-objects as their shoots; and below, in the world of men, its roots stretch forth, binding through action.
t.15.3: Its form is not perceived here as such, nor its end, nor its beginning, nor its foundation; having cut down this aśvattha tree, with its firmly grown roots, by the strong axe of non-attachment,
t.15.4: Then that state must be sought, having gone to which they do not return again: 'I take refuge in that very primal Puruṣa, from whom the ancient activity has streamed forth.'
t.15.5: Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, ever devoted to the Self, with desires wholly turned away, released from the pairs of opposites known as pleasure and pain, the undeluded go to that imperishable state.
t.15.6: Neither the sun nor the moon nor fire illumines that; having gone there, they do not return. That is my supreme abode.
t.15.7: An eternal portion of Myself alone, having become the living soul in the world of living beings, draws to itself the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which abide in material nature.
t.15.8: Whatever body the lord obtains, and whatever body he departs from, he goes on taking these with him, as the wind carries scents from their source.
t.15.9: Presiding over the ear, the eye, touch, taste and smell, and the mind as well, this one enjoys the objects of the senses.
t.15.10: Whether departing, or remaining, or experiencing while joined with the guṇas, the deluded do not perceive him; those who have the eye of knowledge see him.
t.15.11: Striving yogins see him established in the self; but those of unperfected self, lacking discernment, do not see him, even though they strive.
t.15.12: The radiance that, residing in the sun, illumines the whole world, the radiance that is in the moon and that which is in fire, know that radiance to be mine.
t.15.13: Entering the earth, I sustain all beings by My vital energy; and becoming Soma, whose very nature is sap, I nourish all the plants.
t.15.14: Becoming Vaiśvānara, the fire of digestion, I abide in the bodies of living beings, and, joined with prāṇa and apāna, I digest the four kinds of food.
t.15.15: And I am seated in the heart of all; from Me come memory, knowledge, and their removal. By all the Vedas it is I alone who am to be known; I am indeed the maker of the Vedānta and the knower of the Vedas.
t.15.16: There are two Puruṣas in this world, the perishable and the imperishable. The perishable is all beings, and the unchanging one is called the imperishable.
t.15.17: But the highest Person is another, declared to be the Supreme Self, the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them.
t.15.18: Since I transcend the perishable and am higher even than the imperishable, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as Puruṣottama, the Supreme Person.
t.15.19: He who, free from delusion, thus knows me as the Supreme Person, he, knowing all, worships me with his whole being, O Bhārata.
t.15.20: Thus has this most secret teaching been spoken by me, O sinless one. Having understood this, one becomes truly wise and has accomplished all that is to be done, O Bhārata.
t.16.1: The Blessed Lord said: Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, charity, self-restraint and sacrifice, study of the scriptures, austerity, and uprightness.
t.16.2: Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquility, absence of slander, compassion toward all beings, freedom from greed, gentleness, modesty, and steadiness.
t.16.3: Vigor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, freedom from malice, and absence of excessive pride: these, O Bhārata, belong to one born to the divine endowment.
t.16.4: Hypocrisy, arrogance and excessive pride, anger and harshness too, and ignorance, O Pārtha, belong to one who is born to the demonic endowment.
t.16.5: The divine endowment is considered to lead to liberation, the demonic to bondage. Do not grieve, Pāṇḍava; you are born to the divine endowment.
t.16.6: There are two kinds of created beings in this world, the divine and the demonic. The divine has been described at length; now hear from me, O Pārtha, about the demonic.
t.16.7: Demonic people know neither what is to be done nor what is to be refrained from; neither purity nor good conduct nor truth is found in them.
t.16.8: They say that the world is without truth, without foundation, without a Lord, not brought about by any orderly causation; what else is it but caused by desire?
t.16.9: Holding fast to this view, these lost souls of little understanding, doers of cruel deeds and enemies of the world, rise up for its destruction.
t.16.11: Clinging to immeasurable anxiety that ends only with death, holding the enjoyment of desires as the highest aim, they are convinced that this is all there is.
t.16.10: Taking refuge in insatiable desire, filled with hypocrisy, pride and arrogance, having seized upon false notions through delusion, they act with impure vows.
t.16.12: Bound by hundreds of fetters of hope and wholly devoted to desire and anger, they strive by unjust means to amass hoards of wealth for the gratification of their desires.
t.16.13: "This has been gained by me today; this desire I shall attain. This wealth is mine, and this too shall be mine again."
t.16.14: That enemy has been slain by me, and I shall slay others too. I am the lord, I am the enjoyer; I am accomplished, mighty, and happy.
t.16.15: "I am wealthy and of noble birth; who else is there equal to me? I will sacrifice, I will give, I will rejoice": thus they speak, deluded by ignorance.
t.16.16: Bewildered by many thoughts, enveloped in the net of delusion, and attached to the enjoyment of desires, they fall into a foul hell.
t.16.17: Self-conceited, obstinate, filled with the pride and intoxication of wealth, they perform sacrifices that are sacrifices in name only, with hypocrisy and without regard for the prescribed rules.
t.16.18: Given over to egoism, force, arrogance, desire and anger, these malicious ones hate Me, who dwell in their own bodies and in the bodies of others.
t.16.19: Those hateful and cruel ones, the vilest of men, the inauspicious, I perpetually hurl into the cycles of rebirth, into demonic wombs alone.
t.16.20: Having fallen into demoniac wombs, deluded birth after birth, never attaining Me, O Kaunteya, they then go to the lowest state.
t.16.21: Threefold is this gate of hell, destructive of the self: desire, anger, and likewise greed. Therefore one should abandon these three.
t.16.22: A man who is released from these three gates of darkness, O Kaunteya, practises what is good for himself, and thereby he goes to the supreme goal.
t.16.23: He who casts aside the injunctions of scripture and acts according to the impulse of desire attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal.
t.16.24: Therefore let scripture be your authority in determining what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. Having known the action declared by the ordinances of scripture, you should perform it here in this world.
t.17.1: Arjuna said: Those who, setting aside the ordinances of scripture, offer sacrifice endowed with faith, what is their standing, O Kṛṣṇa? Is it sattva, or rajas, or tamas?
t.17.2: The Blessed Lord said: The faith of embodied beings is of three kinds, born of their own nature: sāttvic, rājasic, and tāmasic. Hear about it.
t.17.3: The faith of each person, O Bhārata, is in accordance with his nature. This person is made of faith; whatever his faith is, that indeed is he.
t.17.4: Those of sāttvika nature worship the gods; those of rājasa nature worship the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas; and the others, people of tāmasa nature, worship the departed spirits and the hosts of ghosts.
t.17.5: Those people who practice terrible austerity not enjoined by the scriptures, joined with hypocrisy and egoism, and possessed of the force of desire and passion,
t.17.6: Senseless, they torment the aggregate of elements dwelling in the body, and Me also, who dwell within the body; know them to be of demoniac resolve.
t.17.7: Even the food that is dear to everyone is of three kinds, and so too are sacrifice, austerity and giving. Hear now this distinction among them.
t.17.8: Foods that increase life, vitality, strength, health, happiness and satisfaction, that are savory, rich, substantial and pleasing to the heart, are dear to the sāttvika person.
t.17.10: Food that is stale, tasteless, putrid and left overnight, and that which is leftover and impure, is dear to the tāmasic person.
t.17.9: Foods that are bitter, sour, salty, excessively hot, pungent, dry and burning are dear to the passionate person; they bring pain, grief and disease.
t.17.11: That sacrifice which is offered according to the scriptural injunction by those who do not desire its fruit, having fixed the mind on the thought that it ought simply to be offered, is sāttvika.
t.17.12: But that which is offered with an eye to its fruit, and also for the sake of ostentation, O best of the Bharatas, know that sacrifice to be rājasic.
t.17.13: A sacrifice performed without regard to the scriptural injunctions, in which no food is distributed, which is devoid of sacred mantras, offers no gifts to the priests, and lacks faith, they declare to be of the nature of tamas.
t.17.15: Speech that causes no agitation, that is truthful, pleasant and beneficial, and also the regular practice of sacred recitation, is called austerity of speech.
t.17.14: Worship of the gods, the twice-born, the teachers and the wise, purity, uprightness, celibacy and non-violence: this is called austerity of the body.
t.17.16: Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint, and purity of one's inner being: this is called austerity of the mind.
t.17.17: That threefold austerity, practiced with supreme faith by steadfast men who do not crave its fruit, they call sāttvika.
t.17.18: Austerity that is performed for the sake of gaining respect, honor and reverence, and with ostentation, is here declared to be rājasa, unsteady and impermanent.
t.17.19: That austerity which is performed out of a deluded notion, with torture of oneself, or for the purpose of destroying another, is declared to be tāmasa.
t.17.20: The gift that is given with the thought "it ought to be given," to one who does no service in return, at the proper place and time and to a worthy recipient, that gift is held to be sāttvika.
t.17.21: But that gift which is given for the sake of a return favor, or again with an eye to its fruit, and which is given grudgingly, is held to be rājasa.
t.17.22: That gift which is given at the wrong place and time, and to unworthy recipients, without respect and with contempt, is declared to be tāmasa.
t.17.23: "Oṃ Tat Sat": this is remembered as the threefold designation of Brahman. By it were ordained of old the Brāhmaṇas, the Vedas and the sacrifices.
t.17.24: Therefore, uttering "Om," the expounders of Brahman always undertake their acts of sacrifice, giving, and austerity as enjoined by the scriptural rules.
t.17.25: Uttering "tat" and without aiming at the fruit, those who long for liberation perform the various acts of sacrifice and austerity and the acts of giving.
t.17.26: This word "sat" is used in the sense of reality and in the sense of goodness; likewise, O Pārtha, the word "sat" is applied to a praiseworthy deed.
t.17.27: Steadfastness in sacrifice, in austerity and in giving is also called "sat"; and any action done for that purpose is likewise designated "sat."
t.17.28: Whatever is offered in sacrifice, given, or practised as austerity, or otherwise done without faith, is called asat, O Pārtha; it is of no avail either after death or here.
t.18.1: Arjuna said: O mighty-armed one, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O slayer of Keśin, I wish to know the true nature of renunciation and of relinquishment, each separately.
t.18.2: The Blessed Lord said: The sages know saṃnyāsa to be the laying aside of actions prompted by desire; the discerning declare tyāga to be the relinquishing of the fruits of all actions.
t.18.4: Hear from me my conclusion there, concerning renunciation, O best of the Bhāratas; for renunciation, O tiger among men, has been declared to be of three kinds.
t.18.3: Some wise men declare that action, being full of fault, should be abandoned; and others say that acts of sacrifice, giving, and austerity should not be abandoned.
t.18.5: Acts of sacrifice, giving, and austerity are not to be abandoned; they must indeed be performed. Sacrifice, giving, and austerity are purifiers of the wise.
t.18.6: But even these actions should be performed, abandoning attachment and the fruits; this, O Pārtha, is my decided and supreme conviction.
t.18.7: But the renunciation of prescribed action is not proper; its abandonment out of delusion is declared to be tāmasic.
t.18.8: One who abandons an action merely because it is painful, out of fear of bodily hardship, performs a rājasic renunciation and does not obtain the fruit of renunciation at all.
t.18.9: When prescribed action is performed, O Arjuna, simply because it ought to be done, abandoning attachment and the fruit as well, that relinquishment is regarded as sāttvika.
t.18.10: The relinquisher, pervaded by goodness, wise, with his doubts cut away, does not hate disagreeable action, nor does he cling to agreeable action.
t.18.11: Indeed, it is not possible for one who bears a body to abandon actions entirely; but he who abandons the fruit of action is called a true renunciant.
t.18.12: The threefold fruit of action, undesired, desired, and mixed, accrues after death to those who have not renounced, but never to those who have renounced.
t.18.13: Learn from me, O mighty-armed one, these five causes for the accomplishment of all actions, which are declared in the Sāṃkhya doctrine, the final conclusion.
t.18.14: The seat of action, and likewise the doer, the instruments of various kinds, the many distinct activities, and here divine providence as the fifth.
t.18.15: Whatever action a man undertakes by body, speech and mind, whether right or contrary, these five are its causes.
t.18.16: This being so, whoever, owing to an untrained understanding, sees the self alone as the doer, that man of perverse mind does not see.
t.18.18: Knowledge, the object to be known, and the knower form the threefold impulse to action; the instrument, the action, and the agent form the threefold composition of action.
t.18.17: He whose state of being is not egoistic, whose understanding is not tainted, even though he slays these worlds, he does not slay and is not bound.
t.18.19: Knowledge, action, and the doer are declared in the enumeration of the guṇas to be of three kinds only, according to the distinction of the guṇas; hear of these too, just as they are.
t.18.20: That knowledge by which one sees in all beings a single imperishable reality, undivided among the divided, know that knowledge to be sāttvika.
t.18.21: But know that knowledge to be rājasa which, by way of separateness, perceives in all beings manifold entities of distinct kinds.
t.18.23: Action that is prescribed, free from attachment, performed without love or hatred by one who does not crave its fruit, that is called sāttvika.
t.18.22: But that knowledge which clings to one single task as if it were the whole, without reason, without grasp of the truth, and narrow, is declared to be tāmasa.
t.18.24: But that action which is performed by one desiring the fulfilment of desires, or again by one with egotism, and with great strain, is declared to be rājasa.
t.18.25: That action which is undertaken out of delusion, without regard for its consequences, the loss and harm it causes, or one's own capacity, is said to be tāmasa.
t.18.26: The doer who is free from attachment, who does not speak of himself, who is endowed with steadfastness and zeal, and who is unchanged in success and failure is called sāttvika.
t.18.27: The doer who is passionate, eager for the fruits of his actions, greedy, violent by nature and impure, and given to joy and grief, is declared to be rājasa.
t.18.28: The doer who is undisciplined, vulgar, obstinate, deceitful, malicious, lazy, despondent, and procrastinating is said to be tāmasic.
t.18.29: Hear now, O Dhanaṃjaya, the threefold division of understanding and of steadfastness according to the guṇas, as it is declared fully and in its distinctness.
t.18.30: The understanding that knows action and renunciation, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, fear and fearlessness, bondage and liberation, that understanding, O Pārtha, is sāttvika.
t.18.31: That understanding by which one knows wrongly dharma and adharma, and also what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, is rājasic, O Pārtha.
t.18.32: That understanding, O Pārtha, which, enveloped in darkness, regards adharma as dharma and sees all things in reverse, is tāmasic.
t.18.33: The steadfastness by which, through unwavering yoga, one holds in check the workings of the mind, the vital breath and the senses, that steadfastness, O Pārtha, is sāttvika.
t.18.35: That steadfastness by which a foolish person does not let go of sleep, fear, grief, despondency and arrogance, O Pārtha, is tāmasic.
t.18.34: But the steadfastness by which, O Arjuna, one holds fast to dharma, pleasure and wealth, craving their fruits out of attachment, that steadfastness, O Pārtha, is of the nature of rajas.
t.18.36: But now hear from me, O bull among the Bhāratas, of the threefold happiness, in which one delights through practice and reaches the end of sorrow.
t.18.37: That which at first is like poison but in the end is like nectar, that happiness is declared to be sāttvika, born of the clarity of one's own understanding.
t.18.38: That happiness which arises from the contact of the senses with their objects, which at first is like nectar but in the end is like poison, is declared to be rājasic.
t.18.39: That happiness which deludes the self both at the beginning and in its consequence, arising from sleep, sloth and heedlessness, is declared to be tāmasa.
t.18.40: There is no being, either on earth or again in heaven among the gods, that could be free from these three guṇas born of prakṛti.
t.18.41: The duties of brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and vaiśyas, as well as of śūdras, O scorcher of foes, are distinguished according to the guṇas that arise from their own nature.
t.18.42: Tranquility, self-restraint, austerity, purity, forbearance, and uprightness, knowledge, realized wisdom, and faith in the hereafter: these are the duties of a Brāhmaṇa, born of his own nature.
t.18.43: Heroism, vigor, steadfastness, skill, and also not fleeing in battle, generosity, and the bearing of a lord: these are the duties of the Kṣatriya, born of his own nature.
t.18.44: Agriculture, cattle-tending and trade are the work of the Vaiśya, born of his own nature; and work consisting of service is likewise the work of the Śūdra, born of his own nature.
t.18.45: Each man, devoted to his own particular work, attains perfection. Hear now how one who is intent on his own duty finds perfection.
t.18.46: By worshipping through his own work Him from whom all beings have their origin and by whom all this is pervaded, a man attains perfection.
t.18.47: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work ordained by one's own nature, one incurs no sin.
t.18.48: One should not abandon the work that is born with one's nature, O Kaunteya, even though it is flawed; for all undertakings are enveloped by fault, as fire is by smoke.
t.18.49: He whose understanding is unattached everywhere, who has mastered himself, and from whom longing has departed, attains through renunciation the supreme perfection of freedom from action.
t.18.50: Learn from me in brief, O Kaunteya, how one who has attained perfection attains Brahman, which is the supreme culmination of knowledge.
t.18.52: Dwelling in solitude, eating lightly, with speech, body and mind restrained, ever intent on the yoga of meditation, and taking full refuge in dispassion.
t.18.51: Endowed with a purified intellect, holding firm and restraining the self, abandoning sound and the other objects of the senses, and casting aside attachment and aversion,
t.18.53: Having cast off egotism, force, arrogance, desire, anger and possessiveness, free from the sense of 'mine' and at peace, he becomes fit for becoming Brahman.
t.18.54: Having become Brahman, serene in self, he neither grieves nor desires; equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion to me.
t.18.55: By devotion he comes to know Me truly, how great I am and who I am; then, having known Me truly, he enters into That immediately thereafter.
t.18.56: Even while always performing all actions, one who takes refuge in me attains, by my grace, the eternal, imperishable abode.
t.18.57: Mentally renouncing all actions in Me, holding Me as the supreme goal, and taking refuge in the yoga of understanding, be constantly with your mind fixed on Me.
t.18.58: With your mind fixed on me, you will cross over all difficulties by my grace. But if, out of egoism, you will not listen, you will perish.
t.18.59: If, taking refuge in egoism, you think, "I will not fight," vain is this resolve of yours; your own nature will compel you.
t.18.60: O Kaunteya, bound by your own action born of your own nature, that which you do not wish to do out of delusion, you will do even against your will.
t.18.61: The Lord dwells in the region of the heart of all beings, O Arjuna, causing all beings, as if mounted on a machine, to revolve by his māyā.
t.18.62: Go to Him alone for refuge with your whole being, O Bhārata. By His grace you will attain supreme peace and the eternal abode.
t.18.63: Thus has knowledge more secret than all secrets been declared to you by me. Reflect on it fully, and then do as you wish.
t.18.64: Hear again my supreme word, the most secret of all: you are dearly loved by me, and therefore I shall tell you what is for your good.
t.18.65: Fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, sacrifice to me, bow down to me. You will come to me alone; this I truly promise you, for you are dear to me.
t.18.66: Abandoning all dharmas, go to me alone for refuge. I will free you from all sins; do not grieve.
t.18.68: He who shall declare this supreme secret among My devotees, having shown the highest devotion to Me, shall come to Me alone, freed from doubt.
t.18.67: This is never to be spoken by you to one who lacks austerity, nor to one who lacks devotion, nor to one who does not wish to listen, nor to one who speaks ill of me.
t.18.69: And there is none among men who does Me more dear service than he, nor shall there ever be another on earth dearer to Me than he.
t.18.70: And whoever will study this sacred dialogue of ours, by him I would be worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge; such is my conviction.
t.18.71: And even the man who merely listens to it with faith and without envy, he too, released, would attain the auspicious worlds of those whose deeds are meritorious.
t.18.72: Has this been heard by you, Pārtha, with a one-pointed mind? Has your delusion born of ignorance been destroyed, Dhanaṃjaya?
t.18.73: Arjuna said: Destroyed is my delusion, and by Your grace, O Acyuta, I have regained my memory. I stand firm, my doubts gone; I will do as You say.
t.18.74: Saṃjaya said: Thus have I heard this wondrous dialogue between Vāsudeva and the great-souled Pārtha, which makes the hair stand on end.
t.18.75: By the grace of Vyāsa I have heard this supreme and secret yoga from Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, as He Himself declared it directly.
t.18.76: O King, as I recall again and again this wondrous and holy dialogue between Keśava and Arjuna, I rejoice over and over.
t.18.77: And remembering again and again that most wondrous form of Hari, great is my astonishment, O King, and I rejoice again and again.
t.18.78: Wherever there is Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, and wherever there is Pārtha, the bearer of the bow, there will surely be fortune, victory, prosperity and sound conduct; such is my conviction.
